entities.summary: Olav Magnusson of Norway was king of Norway from 1103 to 1115, succeeding his father Magnus Barefoot. He was the son of Magnus Barefoot and Sigrid, daughter of Saxe of Vik. During his reign, Olav Magnusson strengthened Norway's relationship with Denmark and secured a significant trade agreement with the Hanseatic League. He also promoted the spread of Christianity in Norway, which would later shape the country's identity. Olav Magnusson's legacy can be seen in the modern Norwegian monarchy, which continues to be influenced by the country's Viking heritage. The Viking ships that Olav Magnusson had built were later used in the Danelaw, a region of England that was under Viking control. In his later years, Olav Magnusson was involved in a dispute with King Henry I of England over the succession of the Danelaw. Despite his efforts, Olav Magnusson was unable to secure the throne, and he died in 1115. Olav Magnusson's death marked the end of an era in Norway, and he was remembered as a strong and wise leader who had secured a promising future for his country. Olav Magnusson's legacy can still be seen in the many cultural and historical artifacts that remain in Norway today.
